'''Cuiba''' or '''Cuiva''' is a [[Guahiban languages|Guahiban]] language that is spoken by about 2,300 people in [[Colombia]] and additional 650 in [[Venezuela]].  More than half of Cuiba speakers are monolingual, and in Colombia there is a 45% literacy rate.{{Citation needed|date=May 2016}}<ref>{{Cite news |title=Cuiba Language (CUI) – L1 & L2 Speakers, Status, Map, Endangered Level & Official Use {{!}} Ethnologue Free |url=https://www.ethnologue.com/language/cui/ |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20251210052145/https://www.ethnologue.com/language/cui/ |archive-date=2025-12-10 |access-date=2025-12-29 |work=Ethnologue (Free All) |language=en-US}}</ref> Cuiva is also referred to as '''Cuiba''', '''Cuiba-Wámonae''', '''Kuiva''', '''Chiricoa''', '''Hiwi''', and '''Maiben'''. In Colombia, Cuiva is spoken among those who live and who are born surrounding the Colombian rivers, [[Casanare River|Meta Casanare]] and [[Capanaparo River|Capanaparo]]. The [[Cuiba ethnic group]] is often found in the [[Casanare Department]]. In Venezuela the language is spoken in the state of [[Apure]], one of the states that border with Colombia, and which is found alongside the Capanaparo river.

==History==
{{Unreferenced section|date=September 2025}}
The term Cuiba is usually used to describe the ethnic group itself, although they do not refer to themselves as Cuiba. Most of those who speak the Cuiba language are monolingual, which is why the language is threatened seeing as the ethnic population itself is only approximately 2,950 and continues to decrease. The Cuiba ethnic group are characterized as being [[hunter-gatherer]]s, who live a nomadic lifestyle in small bands along the borders of Colombia and Venezuela. Before 1967, the Cuiba were spread across the [[Meta River]] tributaries: Casanare, [[Água Clara River|Agua Clara]], [[Ariporo River|Ariporo]], [[Unchadia River|Unchadia]], [[Arauca River|Arauca]], and Capanaparo. For the most part although the groups of Cuiba today are much smaller, they continue to occupy what is left of the areas around the rivers.{{Citation needed|date=May 2016}}

The banks of the Casanare, Agua Clara, Ariporo, Unchadia, Arauca, and Capanaparo are for the most part known as Cuiba territory and there has been no evidence stating that the Cuiba have occupied other territory but their own. The Cuiba have gone through many wars and invasions, which have slightly influenced Cuiba political and cultural practices at some point. Although the Europeans have left, some [[Spanish language|Spanish]] words survived. There is no evidence showing where the Spanish words were originated. There have been many attempts after the [[Spanish conquest of New Granada|1533 invasion]] attempting to remove the Cuiba from their territory, but although the Cuiba have a small population their culture has largely remained unchanged.

==Dialects==
{{Unreferenced section|date=September 2025}}
There are 8 dialects in Colombia and Venezuela known as:
*Chiricoa
*Masiware (Masiguare)
*Chiripo (Siripu, Wapiwi)
*Yara huuraxi-Capanapara
*Mayayero
*Monchuelo-Casanare-Cuiba
*Tampiwi (Mariposas)
*Amarawa (Amorua)
